modules.title: Git and GitHub basics
modules.summary: Build a beginner foundation in version control, everyday Git commands, and the GitHub platform.

lessons.title: Version control: the team time machine
lessons.summary: Learn why version control matters and how Git concepts such as repositories, commits, branches, and merges fit together.
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose and benefits of version control
Explain distributed version control in beginner-friendly terms
Identify repositories, commits, branches, merges, and merge conflicts
lessons.explanation:
Imagine Tailwind Traders updates a product page minutes before a launch. A typo slips in, a designer has a better image, and a teammate is still changing prices. Without **version control**, the team is emailing files named `final-v7-really-final.md`. With Git, every meaningful change becomes part of a tracked history.

A **version control system** records what changed, who changed it, and why. Git is distributed: each contributor can have a full local copy of the repository and its history, so people can work independently and synchronize later. The shared copy on GitHub is often called the **remote** repository, while the copy on your computer is local.

A **repository** is the project container. A **commit** is a snapshot with a message. A **branch** is a line of work, often used for a feature or fix. A **merge** combines one branch into another. If Git cannot safely combine edits to the same part of a file, it reports a **merge conflict** so a person can choose the final content.

GitHub adds collaboration around this Git history: hosted repositories, web-based discussion, pull requests, review, permissions, and notifications. In the **Clone, commit, push, and open a pull request with Git CLI** lab, you practise moving from a local change to a reviewed pull request.

terminology.definition: A system that tracks file changes over time.
A project and its revision history.
A saved snapshot with a message.
Combining changes from one branch into another.

lessons.businessScenario: Tailwind Traders keeps website copy, product images, and deployment notes in one repository. Marketing can update wording on a branch while engineering fixes a bug on another branch.
lessons.technicalExample: A simple history might be: `main` has commit `A`; Priya creates `feature/banner`; she commits `B`; after review, the team merges `feature/banner` into `main` so the launch branch includes the banner change.

misconception.myth: Git is only for professional developers.
misconception.reality: Git tracks text files well, but the idea is useful for documentation, configuration, lesson content, scripts, and many other collaborative files.

lessons.examTakeaway: Watch for scenarios that ask why teams use Git: audit history, safe parallel work, recovery of earlier versions, and collaboration without overwriting each other.
lessons.recap: Version control gives teams a reliable history. Git is distributed, repositories hold projects, commits record snapshots, branches isolate work, and merges bring work together.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of Git as a shared notebook with a rewind button. Everyone can write in their own copy, label their changes, then agree which pages go into the official notebook.
lessons.anotherExample: A finance team stores policy documents in Git. Each policy update uses a branch, a commit message explains the change, and a pull request records the approval conversation.

lessons.title: Everyday Git commands with real examples
lessons.summary: Practise the Git commands beginners see most often: clone, status, add, commit, push, pull, branch, switch, checkout, and merge.
learningObjectives: Choose the correct Git command for common tasks
Explain working tree, staging area, local repository, and remote repository
Recognize a safe beginner workflow from clone to push
lessons.explanation:
The command line can feel like a secret language until you connect each command to a job. In Git, most daily work follows a loop: get a copy, inspect it, make changes, stage the right files, commit, synchronize, and repeat.

Use `git clone https://github.com/contoso-labs/inventory-api.git` to create a local copy of a remote repository. Use `git status` often; it tells you the current branch, changed files, and whether changes are staged. `git add docs/health.md` moves a file into the staging area for the next commit. `git commit -m "Add health endpoint notes"` records the staged changes locally. `git push -u origin feature/health-endpoint` publishes a local branch to the remote. `git pull` fetches remote changes and integrates them into your current branch.

For branches, `git branch` lists branches, `git switch -c feature/name` creates and switches to a new branch, and older examples may use `git checkout -b feature/name`. `git merge feature/name` combines another branch into your current branch. The safest habit is to check `git status` before and after important steps.

The **Clone, commit, push, and open a pull request with Git CLI** lab turns these commands into muscle memory without touching a real repository.

terminology.definition: The set of changes selected for the next commit.
A hosted repository location such as GitHub.
Send local commits to a remote.
Bring remote changes into your current branch.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso Labs asks Alex to add health endpoint notes. Alex clones the repository, creates a branch, writes the file, stages it, commits it, pushes the branch, and opens a pull request.
lessons.technicalExample:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/contoso-labs/inventory-api.git
cd inventory-api
git switch -c feature/health-endpoint
git status
git add docs/health.md
git commit -m "Add health endpoint notes"
git push -u origin feature/health-endpoint
```

misconception.myth: A commit automatically sends my work to GitHub.
misconception.reality: A commit saves work in the local repository. You use `git push` to publish commits to the remote repository.

lessons.examTakeaway: Command-selection questions usually test the verb: clone copies, status inspects, add stages, commit records locally, push publishes, pull integrates remote work.
lessons.recap: Git commands are less mysterious when you map them to the workflow: copy, inspect, stage, save, publish, update, branch, and merge.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Picture packing a suitcase. `git add` chooses what goes in the suitcase, `git commit` closes and labels it, and `git push` sends it to the shared destination.
lessons.anotherExample: A documentation writer uses `git pull` before editing so their branch starts from the latest shared updates, then commits only the changed Markdown file.

lessons.title: Working with GitHub: platform, clients, and Markdown
lessons.summary: Understand what GitHub adds on top of Git, account and plan concepts, GitHub Desktop, GitHub Mobile, and GitHub Flavored Markdown.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between Git and GitHub
Describe GitHub account and plan concepts without memorizing prices
Recognize when to use GitHub Desktop, GitHub Mobile, and Markdown
lessons.explanation:
Git is the version control engine; GitHub is the collaboration platform around it. Git can run locally on your computer. GitHub hosts repositories and adds identity, organizations, enterprise management, pull requests, issues, discussions, notifications, documentation, and web-based review.

At a feature level, GitHub accounts organize access. A **user account** represents a person. An **organization account** groups people and repositories for a team. An **enterprise account** centrally manages multiple organizations. GitHub plans affect which features are available, but fundamentals questions should focus on capabilities, not prices.

You can work with GitHub in several clients. Use the web UI for repository settings, issues, pull requests, and quick edits. Use **GitHub Desktop** when you want a visual local Git workflow without memorizing commands. Use **GitHub Mobile** for quick triage: reviewing notifications, commenting on issues and pull requests, and staying responsive away from a desk.

GitHub communication relies heavily on **GitHub Flavored Markdown**. Markdown turns plain text into headings, lists, links, tables, code blocks, task lists, and references. Clear Markdown makes issues and pull requests easier to scan. The GitHub flow appears here as the common collaboration rhythm: branch, commit, open a pull request, review, and merge. You practise the repository side of that flow in the **Create a repository, branch, and pull request on GitHub** lab.

terminology.definition: A platform for hosting Git repositories and collaborating around them.
An account for teams and shared repositories.
A desktop client for a visual local Git workflow.
Plain-text formatting syntax used across GitHub.

lessons.businessScenario: Wide World Importers has writers, developers, and release managers. Developers may prefer Git commands, writers may prefer GitHub Desktop, and managers may use GitHub Mobile to review notifications during travel.
lessons.technicalExample:
A pull request description might use Markdown:

```markdown
## Summary
- Adds health endpoint notes
- Updates README task list

Closes #42
```

misconception.myth: GitHub and Git are the same product.
misconception.reality: Git is the version control system. GitHub uses Git and adds hosted repositories plus collaboration, review, and management features.

lessons.examTakeaway: Watch for wording that separates local version control from hosted collaboration. Git tracks changes; GitHub hosts and coordinates work around those changes.
lessons.recap: GitHub is the shared workspace around Git. Accounts control identity and ownership, clients support different ways of working, and Markdown keeps collaboration readable.
lessons.simplerExplanation: If Git is the engine in a delivery van, GitHub is the warehouse, dispatch board, checklist, and conversation log that help the whole team deliver safely.
lessons.anotherExample: A support engineer writes an issue with headings, a task list, and a code block so the developer can reproduce the problem without a meeting.
